title: Ardas before a meal
hook: families say a short Ardas before eating, and in the gurdwara food is offered with an Ardas before it's served

segments.voice: Yesterday, fateh, and your line: the victory is his. Did you pass the credit on to someone? This week the Ardas leaves the gurdwara hall and comes home, starting at the table. Day six hundred thirty-nine.

The plates are down. The dal is steaming, the rotis are stacked under a cloth, and someone's younger brother already has one hand moving. In many Sikh homes, that hand gets a gentle look. Wait. Someone stands, or just folds their hands at the table, and says a short Ardas, sometimes only a few lines, sometimes just Waheguru and a thank-you. Then everyone eats. It takes less than a minute. It happens in kitchens all over the world, every day.
screen: `THE DAL IS STEAMING.` → `ONE HAND ALREADY MOVING.` → `WAIT: A SHORT ARDAS.`

segments.voice: The Ardas we've been walking through line by line is long. But the Ardas isn't only for the gurdwara, and it isn't only the full form. Sikhs pray it short when the moment is short. Before food, the idea is simple: thank the Giver before taking the gift. In the gurdwara, this is done with care. Before langar is served, food from the kitchen is often brought before the Guru Granth Sahib and an Ardas is said over it. Karah prashad, the sweet offering everyone receives, is also blessed with an Ardas, and in many gurdwaras a kirpan is touched to it before it's shared. Only then does the food go out. Even the full Ardas remembers the kitchen. Among the things it asks for is deg teg fateh. Deg is the cooking pot, the cauldron of the free kitchen. Teg is the sword. Victory to both: to the pot that feeds anyone who comes, and to the sword that protects the weak. Food is so central to Sikh life that it sits in the same breath as defense. At home it's simpler. Families vary: a few lines of the Ardas, a quiet Waheguru, a moment of folded hands. What stays the same is the pause. The food is treated as given, not just bought. That pause does something to the meal itself. A plate you've thanked for is hard to waste. It's a little harder to eat in a rush, or in front of a screen. And it reminds the people at the table that somewhere, a langar is serving strangers the same dal.
screen: `THANK THE GIVER BEFORE THE GIFT.` · `LANGAR IS OFFERED FIRST.` · `DEG TEG FATEH: POT AND SWORD.` · `AT HOME: THE PAUSE.` · then, large: `THANKS BEFORE FOOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, a rehearsal for your next meal. Picture the next plate you'll eat from. Picture where it came from: the field, the truck, the store, the hands that cooked it, even if those hands were yours. Let one face come to mind among all those people. Then let yourself feel grateful, plainly, without needing the right words. If you pray, you can say Waheguru, or a line you already know. When the food actually arrives today, pause for one breath before the first bite. The bell holds the time.
Ardas before a meal. Sikhs offer food with an Ardas before it's served in the gurdwara, and many families pause at home with a short Ardas or Waheguru before eating.
Your line: thanks before food. Today, before every meal, even a snack at your desk, pause for one breath and name who it came from. Day six hundred thirty-nine.

howItsDone: In the gurdwara, langar and karah prashad are offered with an Ardas before being served; at home, many Sikh families say a short Ardas or simply Waheguru before eating.
